newsitem.title: USA: DC told that SEC will drop probe of 1994 bonds.
newsitem.headline: DC told that SEC will drop probe of 1994 bonds.

text.p: A top District of Columbia official said on Thursday the city has been told the Securities and Exchange Commission will drop its probe of a city bond offering in late 1994.
"We have heard informally that the SEC probe will be dropped," Thomas Huestis, deputy chief financial officer for finance, said during a televised interview with Reuters Financial TV.
"But we have not heard anything formally from the SEC," Huestis added. SEC enforcement chief William McLucas was unavailable for comment.
Huestis was responding to a question about whether or not SEC's probe of the December 1994 note offering totalling $250 million has "dampened" interest in DC bonds.

"We've already made the change to better disclosure since Tony has gotten here," Huestis added, referring to District CFO Anthony Williams. "He's instilled a belief that disclosure and investor communications is paramount."
"The District did not do a good enough job in the past, but that would never happen again. We are committed to providing first-class ongoing disclosure to our investors," Huestis said.
Huestis said D.C. is "real pleased" with a tax-lien securitization the city closed this week.

"We sold $35 million of delinquent tax liens and secured $25.8 million in proceeds," Huestis said. "It went to the bottom line to reduce our deficit. It shows the District has a sense of urgency of cleaning up its non-performing assets and its real property tax data base."

Asked if he thinks Congress will enact a commuter tax on D.C. workers who live in nearby Virginia and Maryland, Williams said: "It's not on the table. It's not going to happen. We should just give it up and move forward."
Huestis said the District is planning a $150 million general obligation bond issue in February 1997, which will cover the city's capital needs for the current fiscal year.

"The District has targetted about $150 million that it can afford right now for each of the next four years," Huestis said. He added that a $168 million GO offering last fall was "very well received."
"This was our first entry into the long-term bond market for over three years. Our investments are still below investment grade, but were very pleased with the response," Huestis said.
"We were expecting yields 125-to-140 points over high grade (municipal bonds) and we ended up less than 100 basis points over high grade," he said of last fall's offering.
